x-ray: Before Wilhelm Röntgen, X-rays were noticed as an unidentified radiation coming from discharge tubes, by experimenters investigating cathode rays, the energetic electron beams first observed in 1869. Effects attributable to them appeared in many of the early Crookes tubes, invented around 1875. In these tubes a high direct-current voltage accelerated electrons so that they created X-rays when they struck the anode or the glass wall.

On 8 November 1895 Röntgen, a professor of physics, discovered X-rays while experimenting with Lenard tubes and Crookes tubes. On 28 December 1895 he submitted a preliminary communication, On a new kind of ray, to the journal of Würzburg's Physical-Medical Society, the first paper on X-rays. He called the radiation X to indicate an unknown type, and some early texts, taking the X for the Greek capital chi, speak of Chi-rays.

X-rays are electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths from about 10 nanometres to 10 picometres. Photons above about 5 to 10 keV are called hard X-rays and those of lower energy soft X-rays. There is no consensus on the boundary with gamma rays. One practice distinguishes them by source, X-rays coming from electron deexcitation and gamma rays from the decay of atomic nuclei, and another by wavelength.

X-rays are produced whenever charged particles of sufficient energy strike a material. The usual source is an X-ray tube, in which a high voltage accelerates electrons from a hot cathode into a metal target, the anode. In medical tubes the target is usually tungsten or an alloy of tungsten and rhenium. Bones show clearly on a radiograph because their calcium absorbs X-rays efficiently. Detectors were originally photographic plates and later film, and are now mostly digital.

Röntgen saw at once that X-rays could be used in medicine, and on 1 January 1896 he sent a letter to physicians he knew around Europe. The Scottish electrical engineer Alan Archibald Campbell-Swinton was the first after him to make an X-ray photograph, of a hand. By February there were 46 experimenters in North America alone. John Hall-Edwards made the first use under clinical conditions in Birmingham on 11 January 1896, radiographing a needle stuck in an associate's hand, and on 14 February 1896 he was the first to use X-rays in a surgical operation.

The hazards soon appeared, in stories of burns and hair loss. In February 1896 Professor John Daniel and William Lofland Dudley of Vanderbilt University reported hair loss after Dudley was X-rayed with an exposure of one hour. X-rays are ionising radiation and can cause DNA damage, burns, radiation sickness and cancer, yet the same property is used in radiotherapy to kill malignant cells. First-generation cold-cathode tubes of the Crookes type remained in use until about 1920.
xenophon: Xenophon was born in the Athenian deme of Erchia, the son of Gryllus, who belonged to an aristocratic family. The Peloponnesian War was fought through his childhood and youth. Like many wealthy young men of the time he associated with Socrates, and he probably served in the Athenian cavalry. He seems to have stayed in Athens under the Thirty Tyrants and to have fought the democratic insurgents in the civil war of 404 to 403 BCE. Xenophon was invited by Proxenus of Beotia to join the army that Cyrus the Younger was raising against the Persian satrap Tissaphernes.

Cyrus gathered a large army of Persians and Greeks, and the Greeks did not know at first that it was meant against King Artaxerxes II. After Cyrus was killed at the Battle of Cunaxa, the Spartan general Clearchus and four other generals were seized and executed on the invitation of Tissaphernes. The mercenaries, known as the Ten Thousand, then elected new leaders, among them Xenophon.

In the Anabasis he describes the retreat. The Greeks were harassed by Persian missile cavalry, fought the Carduchians in the mountains, forced a crossing of the Centrites River and marched through Armenia in winter without suitable clothing. They reached Trapezus on the Black Sea coast and fought the Colchians before making their way west. The military historian Theodore Ayrault Dodge called Xenophon the father of the system of retreat.

Afterwards Xenophon served with Spartan commanders in Anatolia and joined the campaign of King Agesilaus. Athens banished him for fighting on the Spartan side at the Battle of Coronea in 394 BCE. He received an estate at Scillus, where he lived for twenty-three years until the Elians confiscated it after Sparta's defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE. According to Diogenes Laertius he then moved to Corinth.

Xenophon's whole body of work survives. It includes the Hellenica, which continues Thucydides' account of the Peloponnesian War to 362 BCE and is partial to Sparta, the Cyropaedia, the biography Agesilaus, the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, and short treatises on horsemanship, hunting with dogs and the finances of Athens. His Socratic works are the Memorabilia, Apology, Symposium and Oeconomicus; apart from Plato's, they are the only surviving Socratic dialogues.

The Cyropaedia gives a fictional Cyrus the Great the qualities of an ideal ruler, and it differs from Herodotus on several points of his career. Some scholars read it as a warning that empires hold together only through a ruler of exceptional ability, and as a criticism of Athenian and Spartan ambitions for empire.
xian: Xi'an lies on the Guanzhong Plain in the south-central part of Shaanxi province, on a flood plain made by eight surrounding rivers and streams. It borders the northern foot of the Qin Mountains to the south and the banks of the Wei River to the north. Hua Shan, one of the five sacred Taoist mountains, is about 100 km to the east, and the Loess Plateau lies not far to the north. The climate is temperate, influenced by the East Asian monsoon, with hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters.

The Lantian Man, discovered in 1963 in Lantian County 50 km southeast of the city, dates to at least 500,000 years before the present. Banpo, a Neolithic village found in 1953 on the eastern outskirts, contains the remains of several well-organised settlements carbon dated to 5,600 to 6,700 years ago.

The area became a cultural and political centre of China in the 11th century BCE with the founding of the Zhou dynasty, whose capital stood in the twin settlements of Fengjing and Haojing, together called Fenghao, southwest of the modern city. King Ping of Zhou later moved the capital to Luoyang because of political unrest. After the Warring States period the Qin dynasty, which ruled from 221 to 206 BCE, unified China from its capital at Xianyang, just northwest of Xi'an. Qin Shi Huang ordered the building of the Terracotta Army and his mausoleum, east of the city, almost as soon as he took the throne.

Under the name Chang'an, the city held the position of capital under several of the most important dynasties, including the Western Han, Sui, Northern Zhou and Tang. The present name, 西安, Western Peace, was adopted in 1369 under the early Ming dynasty. Jesuit missionaries recorded it as Si-ngan or Si-ngan-fou, after its status as a prefectural seat. The Qing dynasty set up a walled Manchu banner quarter in the northeast, on the site of the former palace of the Ming Prince of Qin, and a Han banner quarter in the southeast.

Xi'an is the capital of Shaanxi province and the most populous city in Northwestern China. It is counted among China's Five Great Ancient Capitals. The Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor with the Terracotta Army lies near it, and five component sites of the UNESCO-listed Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor are in the city. Chinese Standard Time is set by the National Time Service Center near Lintong.
xinjiang: Xinjiang is split by the Tian Shan mountain range into the Dzungarian Basin in the north and the Tarim Basin in the south. The Karakoram, Kunlun and Tian Shan ranges occupy much of its borders and its western and southern regions. Most of it is uninhabitable desert and dry grassland, and only about 9.7 per cent of the land is fit for habitation, mostly in oases at the foot of the mountains, where the cities lie. Its older English-language names include Chinese Turkestan and East Turkestan, and the Chinese called it Xiyu, the Western Regions.

Crossed by the Northern Silk Road, the Tarim and Dzungaria were known as the Western Regions. At the start of the Han dynasty the region was ruled by the Xiongnu. In the 2nd century BCE Emperor Wu of Han sent Zhang Qian west to seek an alliance with the Yuezhi, and in 60 BCE the Han established the Protectorate of the Western Regions at Wulei. The area, once inhabited by Indo-European Tocharians and Iranian Sakas who followed Buddhism and Zoroastrianism, became Muslim in the 10th century with the conversion of the Kara-Khanid Khanate, which held Kashgar.

The Uyghur state of the Turpan-Urumchi region submitted to Genghis Khan in 1209, and Xinjiang later came under Kaidu, a descendant of Ögedei Khan. In the 18th century the Qing fought the Dzungars for decades; Qing Manchu Bannermen then carried out the Dzungar genocide, nearly eradicating them and depopulating Dzungaria, and by 1759 China controlled both Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin. The two were governed separately until 1884, when the Qing established the province of Xinjiang. After the fall of the Qing in 1912, Yang Zengxin ruled it for the Republic of China until 1928. The region became part of the People's Republic of China in 1949 and an autonomous region in 1955.

Xinjiang, officially the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, is the largest province-level division of China, covering more than 1.6 million square kilometres in the northwest. It is home to the Uyghurs, Han Chinese, Hui, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Mongols and other peoples, with several autonomous prefectures and counties for minorities. Its largest cities include Ürümqi, Turpan, Kashgar and Karamay, and it has substantial oil and mineral reserves.
